newsitem.title: USA: Space groups up security as Okla. trial date nears.
newsitem.headline: Space groups up security as Okla. trial date nears.

text.p: Just days before the second anniversary of the Oklahoma City bombing, NORAD and the U.S. Space Command have taken extra security precautions at their headquarters, a spokeswoman said on Wednesday.

The organisations, which track objects in the sky and are housed in the same mountain complex, cancelled all public tours and placed barricades outside its headquarters due to "possible security concerns," spokeswoman Franki Webster said.

Webster declined to disclose the nature of the security concerns or say whether they were specifically related to the April 19 anniversaries of the Oklahoma City bombing, which killed 168 people, and the 1993 siege at Waco, Texas, where some 80 members of the Branch Davidian cult died in a standoff with federal officials.
She said the Air Force took the action on Tuesday after it learned of possible security concerns. She declined to disclose where the warnings came from.

The Oklahoma City bombing trial of Timothy McVeigh was under way in Denver where security was extremely high. Before the trial began on March 31, concrete barricades were erected around the complex that houses the Denver federal courthouse and the adjacent federal office building.
The North American Aerospace Defence Command Centre, or NORAD, and the U.S. Space Command operate from the interior of Cheyenne Mountain on the western edge of Colorado Springs, Colorado.
Inside the bowels of the mountain, experts were on the lookout for worldwide launches of rockets, missiles and unknown aircraft approaching North America.
Security was always very high at NORAD. People wishing to visit must relinquish cameras, beepers and cellular telephones and must make arrangements ahead of time.
